paragraphs.text: Lesson 5, a diet dilemma.
Nathan gives his friend Matt advice on losing weight.
First, listen to their conversation and answer the comprehension questions.
Then you'll learn the expressions in the dialogue.
Oh man, I can't believe this.
What a drag.
What's with you?
Coach Davis just put me on a diet.
He said I'm four pounds over my weight class.
If I don't shed four pounds, I won't be able to wrestle in the state tournament.
So what's the big deal?
Lay off the potato chips, jog a few miles, and drop the pounds.
It's not like you have to lose 50 pounds or anything.
Four pounds shouldn't be too hard.
You don't get it.
My Aunt May is in town.
Man, oh man.
She's been cooking up a storm.
And if you refuse to eat, she cries.
Yeah, I remember your Aunt May.
Didn't she just get divorced or something?
Yeah, now she's using food to fill the void.
Unfortunately, she's making everyone else eat with her.
Last night, Aunt May made me eat three pieces of pecan pie.
If I continue at this rate, I'll be as fat as a blimp in no time.
I guess you do have a problem.
Of course you don't want to hurt your Aunt's feelings, but you can't let her stop you from
making the wrestling tournament.
You're the best wrestler in your weight class.
Sure am.
But if I don't get out of Aunt May's food binge, I'll be wrestling in the sumo weight
class pretty soon.
Seems to me like you're going to have to tell your Aunt May to back off somehow.
Just explain the situation to her.
I'm sure she'll understand.
I'm not so sure.
She's really into this cooking thing.
And I hate to say it, but she's already pretty plump around the waist too.
Hey, I got an idea.
Let me hear it dude.
I'll take anything at this point.
Your Aunt May is into cooking to help her cope with her divorce.
So if you can't beat her, join her.
But I'm trying to lose the weight, not gain it.
Shut up and listen.
Just ask your Aunt May to start cooking healthy, fat free meals.
Stuff with low carbs and high end protein.
Well, that might work.
But my Aunt May is really into pasta and the sweets that follow.
I don't even want to know how many calories those slices of pecan pie had.
But you can surely suggest different meals.
Well, I guess it wouldn't hurt.
Look, Matt, the team needs you.
So either you open your mouth at dinner time and suggest healthy meals or else say goodbye
to making the state tournament.
I know, I know.
Maybe I can check out a healthy cookbook at the library and take it home with me.
Now you're talking.
I'm sure you'll find a way to drop four pounds without hurting your Aunt's feelings.
Don't stress about it.
Come on.
I'll walk over to the library with you.
Let's learn the vocabulary from today's conversation.
Matt starts off by saying, what a drag.
This is a slang phrase which means this is annoying.
Nathan asks, what's with you?
What's with you is an informal way to ask what's the problem you're having.
Another way to say this is, what's the matter?
Matt says he needs to shed four pounds in order to compete in the state tournament.
Shed four pounds means to lose four pounds.
Nathan asks, so what's the big deal?
This expression, what's the big deal, means this isn't such a big problem or issue.
Nathan is saying that Matt shouldn't be worried because four pounds is not much to worry about.
Nathan suggests lay off the potato chips.
This expression, lay off the potato chips means eat less of or stop eating so many potato
chips.
But Matt replies, you don't get it.
This expression, you don't get it, means you don't understand.
It's a more informal way to say it.
Matt's Aunt May is in town and he says she's been cooking up a storm.
This means she's been cooking a lot.
Matt's Aunt May just got divorced and now she's using food to fill the void.
Fill the void means to feel better after a loss.
Basically, she's using food to comfort her and make her feel better after her divorce.
So Matt has been eating a lot.
He says, if I continue at this rate, I'll be as fat as a blimp in no time.
A blimp is a type of aircraft that's filled with air.
It has a round fat shape, so to be fat as a blimp means extremely fat.
Nathan warns Matt, you can't let her stop you from making the wrestling tournament.
Making the wrestling tournament means becoming eligible to participate in the tournament.
And Matt says, if I don't get out of Aunt May's food binge, I'll be wrestling in the sumo weight class pretty soon.
This word, binge means eating too much or eating an excessive amount.
So Nathan says, seems to me you're going to have to tell your Aunt May to back off.
The phrasal verb back off means stop being so aggressive or pushy.
Matt is not so sure that his Aunt will understand.
He says, she's really into this cooking thing.
She's really into, is an informal way to say she's very interested in or she's very dedicated.
And Matt adds, I hate to say it, but she's already pretty plump around the waist too.
The word plump means fat.
Nathan has an idea, and Matt says, let me hear it dude.
This means let me, let me hear it.
But the two words let me run together and it sounds like lemme, lemme hear it dude.
Nathan says, your Aunt May is into cooking to help her cope with her divorce.
The phrasal verb cope with means to handle or manage emotionally.
And Nathan suggests if you can't beat her, join her.
Matt protests, but I'm trying to lose weight, not gain it.
And Nathan says, shut up and listen.
Shut up means stop talking.
This is a rather rude way to tell someone to stop talking, and it should only be used between
two close friends who have a good relationship and can joke with each other.
Nathan tells Matt to ask his Aunt May to start cooking healthy, fat-free meals, stuff with low
carbs and high in protein.
The word carbs is short for carbohydrates.
Matt's response to this suggestion is, well, I guess it wouldn't hurt.
This expression, it wouldn't hurt, means it wouldn't have any negative effect, so I might as well try it.
Nathan encourages Matt, look Matt the team needs you, so either you open your mouth at dinner time
and suggest healthy meals, or else say goodbye to making the state tournament.
This expression, say goodbye to making the state tournament, means accept the fact that this opportunity will not happen.
Matt then has an idea.
He says, maybe I can check out a healthy cookbook at the library.
The phrasal verb check out in this context means to borrow a book from the library.
And Nathan says, now you're talking.
This means, now you're saying the right thing, or now you're having a good idea.
And at the end of the dialogue, Matt and Nathan decide to walk to the library together.
That's all the vocabulary from today's conversation.
